replies:
Trainee, your career agent. I’ll run a mock interview for a financial analyst role now.

First question (answer in one or two minutes as you would in the room): 
"Walk me through your resume — highlight the experience most relevant to a financial analyst role and one achievement that shows your analytical impact."

After you answer I will score it on structure, evidence and specificity, give one concrete improvement, then ask the next question. Ready? One short line if you want a different first question.

Score 2/10. Improvement: say the situation, your action with tools and numbers, and the result with a metric. Rewrite it into a 2–3 sentence answer that follows STAR and includes one concrete number. I'll then ask the next question.

Honest score: 3/10.

Why: You moved toward the right shape by naming the model and a check against comps, but the answer still misses most of what interviewers listen for: a clear Situation, a specific Task, the Actions you personally took (with tools or methods), and a measurable Result. There's no timeframe, no scale (revenues, size of model), no tools (Excel, VBA, forecasting method), and no numeric outcome.
One concrete rewrite (2–3 sentences, STAR, with a number) you can use or adapt:
"In a three-month finance rotation at [Company], I rebuilt the company's three-statement model from top-down revenue drivers using Excel and scenario analysis, linking product-unit forecasts to pricing and churn assumptions. I validated the forecasts by comparing them to three public comps and stress-tested downside cases; this reduced our month-ahead forecast error from 15% to 6%."
Concrete improvement to make next: pick a real past project, add the time period and the numerical result you achieved, and name one tool or method you used ([your skill] model, DCF, regression, pivot tables). Then answer the same prompt again and I'll rescore it.

One question: do you have a real project you want me to base the numbers on, or should I assume a plausible internship example for your next draft?

You don't have any Lincoln International items on file yet (no postings, no interviews recorded). The one step that starts that is: paste the interview invite or tell me the interview date/time, format (virtual/in-person), who you'll meet (names/titles), and any materials they asked for.

Prep now: short brief + likely final-round questions, a 3-part story framework to use, two tailored example answers, and a 10-point checklist you can run through before the interview.
Brief (what the final round usually tests)
- Technical competence: accounting, valuation basics, modeling logic, deal experience or case work you did earlier in the process.
- Fit and motivation: why Lincoln, why M&A/IB, teamwork under pressure.
- Behavioral consistency: examples of leadership, problem-solving, attention to detail.
- Commercial judgment: market awareness, deal rationale, client interaction instincts.
- Case/technical exercise: might be a short modeling/valuation task or live case discussion; they’ll probe your assumptions and reasoning.
Use this 3-part story framework for every behavioral answer
1) Situation + Task (one sentence) — set context and your role.  
2) Action (2–3 sentences) — exactly what you did, tools/analyses used, who you worked with.  
3) Outcome (one sentence with a number or clear result) — measurable where possible, plus one short takeaway.
Likely final-round questions (practice these)
- Walk me through your resume / deal experience. (Be crisp: role, scope, result.)
- Tell me about a time you saved time or improved accuracy on a model. (Use the 3-part story.)
- Describe a difficult team conflict and how you handled it.
- Explain an LBO/DCF step-by-step and common sensitivity checks you run.
- Here’s a short case: [they give an extract]. How would you value this company? What assumptions matter most?
- Tell me about a recent deal you read about — why it made sense and what risks you see.
- Why Lincoln over bulge bracket or other boutiques?
- Where do you see yourself in 3–5 years?
- Tell me about a time you missed something or made an error. What did you do?

Two tailored example answers (short, follow the 3-part story)
1) Question: Tell me about a time you improved a model.
- Situation/Task: On [deal/project], our model had inconsistent period links and checks that caused slow edits under tight deadlines. I owned fixing it.  
- Action: I implemented consistent index-based formulas, added reconciliation rows and automated key checks (revenue bridge, working capital roll-forward). I also added a one-page assumptions summary so reviewers could validate inputs quickly. I taught two teammates the new layout.  
- Outcome/Takeaway: The change cut scenario-prep time by ~30% and eliminated a recurring reconciliation error; senior bankers flagged the model as the cleanest in the pitch and used it in client meetings.
2) Question: Why Lincoln International?
- Situation/Task: I want a role where I do client-facing M&A work across mid-market sectors and can take ownership early.  
- Action: I chose Lincoln because of its sector focus, global reach in the middle market, and emphasis on hands-on deal responsibility; I spoke with [if you did, name] and reviewed recent transactions in [sector they cover], which showed early-associate responsibility and cross-border exposure.  
- Outcome/Takeaway: I see Lincoln as the place to develop substantive client and execution skills quickly and contribute to cross-border deals — that matches how I learn best.
Technical refresh checklist (run through these in the 24–48 hrs before)
1) Walk through a DCF from revenue line to terminal value and unlevered free cash flow.
2) Revise LBO basic mechanics: purchase price, debt tranches, interest, covenants, exit year IRR.
3) Do 2-3 quick accretion/dilution / pro-forma math checks.
4) Brush up on comps: selecting comparables, adjusting multiples, control vs. minority.
5) Open Excel and rebuild a simple 3-statement link or model a quick sensitivity table.
6) Re-read your own deals and be ready to explain your role and numbers precisely.
7) Prepare 2-3 thoughtful questions for each interviewer (about deal pipeline, sector strategy, role expectations).
8) Print or have a one-page deal sheet and resume hard copy for in-person; have a clean screen share copy for virtual.
9) Sleep, clear calendar before the interview, and test audio/video 20 minutes ahead (for virtual).
10) Have a concise closing pitch: top strengths, why you, and immediate contributions.

Mock practice offer
- I can run a 20–30 minute mock now: I’ll ask 4–6 final-round questions (mix of behavioral and technical). After each answer you give, I’ll score structure/evidence/specificity and give one concrete improvement. Want to do that now?

replies:
You don't have any applications on file yet. The one step that starts one is: pick a specific job posting (paste the job link or tell me the exact job title and company and city) so I can read it and prepare the application card.

Here is exactly what I will fill, field by field, for the first posting you pick. I will use only facts already confirmed on your profile or words you give me now; anything missing will be shown as [answer needed] and left for you to approve in the application card.
1) Employer / Posting link
- What I will place: the exact link you provided (or the posting's employer name and "link not checked just now" if you only name it).
- Why: so the application opens on the employer's form exactly as the posting requires.

2) Role / Job title
- What I will place: the title exactly as the posting lists it (e.g., "Senior Data Analyst").
- Why: many forms require the posting title exactly.

3) Location / On-site vs Remote
- What I will place: the posting's location text (city, remote, hybrid) and any on-site schedule the posting states (e.g., "On-site 3 days/week").
- Why: to match the employer's location filter and screening questions.
4) Resume to use (PDF persona)
- What I will place: the file name of the resume PDF you choose (e.g., "Resume 2026 DataAnalyst.pdf") or [choose resume] if you have not set one.
- If you want a tailored resume, I will create a PDF from your confirmed facts and put its 7-day private link here.
- Why: employers require a resume file; you approve which one.
5) Cover letter / Application note (short)
- What I will place: one short tailored paragraph (≈80–120 words) speaking to the posting's top needs and your top matching facts, with [brackets] where I lack specifics (hiring manager name, team).
- Example structure I will use:
  - 1 sentence naming the role and where you saw it,
  - 1 sentence 2–3 skills or results that match the posting,
  - 1 sentence why you want this employer/team and your availability.
- Why: many forms have a "cover note" or short answer that screens for fit.
6) Key screening questions (yes/no / short answers)
- What I will place: every required screening question the posting asks (e.g., "Authorized to work in the US?", "Do you have [number]+ years in [your skill]?") with suggested answers.
- If you have not told me the needed facts (work authorization, years of experience, salary expectations, relocation), I will put those fields as [answer needed] and suggest wording.
- Why: these questions often decide automatic disqualification.
7) Attachments
- What I will place: the exact filenames you provide for attachments (resume, cover letter PDF if requested, certifications, transcripts, portfolio PDF).
- Any missing required attachment will be flagged [missing — supply file before submission].
- Why: employers often require specific documents.

8) LinkedIn / Portfolio / GitHub / Personal site
- What I will place: the full URLs you confirm or that appear on your resume; otherwise each will be [add link].
- Why: forms often ask for these links; they must be exact.
9) Availability / Earliest start date
- What I will place: your earliest start date in plain text (e.g., "Available in 2–4 weeks" or a specific date) or [answer needed] if you haven't given one.
- Why: hiring teams use this for scheduling and offers.

10) Desired salary / Salary expectation
- If the posting lists pay, I will recommend a range based on that and mark where it informed the suggestion.
- Why: many forms require this and it can be a knockout.

11) Work authorization / Sponsorship
- What I will place: the exact status you confirm (e.g., "US citizen", "Green Card", "Needs sponsorship") or [work auth needed].
- Why: many employers screen for sponsorship needs.
12) References
- What I will place: either "References available upon request" or 2–3 named references with contact info if you give them now.
- Why: some forms request references; others accept the generic line.

13) Equal Employment / Diversity questions
- What I will place: your answers exactly as you instruct or leave blank/choose the optional selections; I will not guess.
- Why: these are optional and personal.

14) Pre-employment assessments / Code samples
- What I will place: links to code samples, a portfolio, or an indication "[none — will provide on request]" depending on what you give me.
- Why: some postings require initial work samples.
15) Short-answer / Behavioral prompts
- What I will place: fully drafted answers to any required essay fields, each within the posting's stated length limits. I will use the STAR format (Situation, Task, Action, Result) and include measurable results where possible; missing specifics will be bracketed.
- Example: "Tell us about a time you improved a process" → a 3–4 sentence STAR answer with a numeric result if you confirm the numbers.
16) Confirmation checkbox / Signature line
- What I will place: the exact affirmation text for review (e.g., "I certify that the information is true"). The browser requires you to check or sign it yourself; I will not sign for you.
- Why: legal confirmation must be completed by you.

17) Final notes / Tailoring checklist (internal to the card)
- What I will place: 2–4 bullet points showing which posting requirements your resume matches (skill keywords, years, certs) and any remaining gaps (e.g., "No direct AWS experience listed — recommend note"). These are internal to the card so you see risk areas before approving.
- Why: you can quickly see whether to apply.
What you'll see in the application card (what you must review and approve in the extension)
- Every field above as labeled inputs with my proposed text.
- Red [answer needed] markers where any fact is missing.
- Links to each file I attach.
- A one-line "Why this wording" note for critical fields (salary, availability, work authorization).
- A final "Approve and queue" button — I will not click it; you must approve it in the Trainee extension.
Assumptions I used for this walkthrough
- You haven't chosen a specific posting yet (so I showed placeholders).
- I will not invent any facts; anything not on file will be bracketed for you to confirm.
- I will not submit anything without your approval in the Trainee extension.

Next step: paste the first posting link you want prepared, or tell me the exact job title, company and city so I can look it up and then prepare this card for your approval. Saved: none yet (no application on file). Is that right?
